interactive_questions.title: Database Sharding & Replication
interactive_questions.prompt: Distribute incoming data across shards based on a sharding key, and observe leader-follower failover behavior when a primary node fails.
interactive_questions.question: Which sharding strategy is generally best for uniform data distribution?
interactive_questions.explanation: Hash-based sharding applies a hash function to the sharding key, ensuring a uniform distribution of data across shards and minimizing hot spots.
interactive_questions.theory_explanation: Database sharding is the process of splitting a large database into smaller, more manageable pieces called shards. Each shard holds a subset of the data. Replication involves copying data from a primary node to one or more follower nodes to ensure high availability. If the primary fails, a follower can be promoted to leader.
interactive_questions.real_world_analogy: Imagine a huge library. Instead of one massive building, you split it into branches by genre (sharding). Then, each branch has a backup warehouse with a copy of its books (replication). If a branch burns down, the warehouse opens to the public (failover).

interactive_questions.title: Event-Driven Architectures
interactive_questions.prompt: Simulate message publishing to topics, visualize consumer groups processing partitions, and handle consumer failure and rebalancing.
interactive_questions.question: In a partitioned message broker (like Kafka), what ensures messages for a specific entity are processed in order?
options: B. Publishing with a consistent routing key
C. Using multiple consumers in a group for the same partition
D. Setting the consumer fetch rate to 1
interactive_questions.answer: B. Publishing with a consistent routing key
interactive_questions.explanation: Publishing messages with the same routing key ensures they are routed to the same partition, guaranteeing order for that key.
interactive_questions.theory_explanation: Event-driven architecture (EDA) promotes asynchronous communication using events. A message broker stores and distributes these events. Topics are often divided into partitions for scalability. Consumer groups read from topics, where each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer within the group. When consumers join or leave, partitions are rebalanced among the group.
interactive_questions.real_world_analogy: Think of a busy restaurant kitchen. Waiters drop orders (events) onto a ticket rail (broker). Several chefs (consumers) pick up tickets to cook. If you want the appetizer and main course for Table 5 cooked in order, you clip them together (routing key) so the same chef handles both.

interactive_questions.title: Load Balancing Algorithms
interactive_questions.prompt: Distribute incoming traffic across servers using different algorithms (Round Robin, Least Connections, IP Hash) and observe server load.
interactive_questions.question: Which load balancing algorithm is best when servers have varying capacities and request processing times are unpredictable?
interactive_questions.explanation: Least Connections dynamically routes traffic to the server with the fewest active connections, handling varying capacities and unpredictable request times effectively.
interactive_questions.theory_explanation: Load balancing distributes network traffic across multiple servers. Algorithms include Round Robin (sequential distribution), Least Connections (sends to least busy server), and IP Hash (sticky sessions based on client IP). This ensures high availability and reliability.
interactive_questions.real_world_analogy: Imagine checkout lines at a grocery store. Round Robin is like sending the next customer to checkout 1, then 2, then 3. Least Connections is like a customer choosing the shortest line.

interactive_questions.title: Rate Limiting Strategies
interactive_questions.prompt: Test different rate limiting algorithms (Token Bucket, Leaky Bucket, Fixed Window) to observe how they handle request spikes.
interactive_questions.question: Which rate limiting algorithm allows for sudden bursts of traffic while maintaining a steady long-term rate?
interactive_questions.explanation: Token Bucket allows bursts of requests up to the bucket's capacity, while refilling tokens at a constant rate.
interactive_questions.theory_explanation: Rate limiting restricts the number of requests a client can make to an API within a specified time frame. Common algorithms include Token Bucket (allows bursts), Leaky Bucket (smooths out traffic), and Fixed/Sliding Window counters. This protects services from overload and DDoS attacks.
interactive_questions.real_world_analogy: Imagine a theme park ride with a queue. The operator lets 10 people in every minute. If 50 people show up at once, only the first 10 get in, and the rest must wait or are turned away.

interactive_questions.title: Caching Strategies
interactive_questions.prompt: Implement different caching strategies (Write-Through, Write-Behind, Cache-Aside) and observe the impact on read/write latency and data consistency.
interactive_questions.question: Which caching strategy ensures that data in the cache and database are always strictly consistent, but incurs higher write latency?
interactive_questions.explanation: Write-Through caching writes data to both the cache and the underlying database simultaneously, ensuring strict consistency but adding the database write latency to the overall response time.
interactive_questions.theory_explanation: Caching temporarily stores frequently accessed data in fast memory to reduce latency. Strategies dictate how data is written: Write-Through (cache and DB together), Write-Behind (cache first, asynchronously to DB), Cache-Aside (application checks cache first, then DB).
interactive_questions.real_world_analogy: Imagine keeping your most used tools on your workbench (cache) instead of in the shed (database). Write-Through is like buying a new tool and putting one on the bench and a spare in the shed immediately.

interactive_questions.title: Consistent Hashing
interactive_questions.prompt: Add and remove nodes in a distributed hash ring and observe how minimal data remapping occurs compared to traditional modulo hashing.
interactive_questions.question: What is the primary benefit of using Consistent Hashing in a distributed caching system?
options: A. It completely eliminates cache misses
B. It minimizes data movement when adding or removing nodes
C. It compresses the cached data
D. It guarantees perfect uniform load distribution without virtual nodes
interactive_questions.answer: B. It minimizes data movement when adding or removing nodes
interactive_questions.explanation: Consistent hashing ensures that when a node is added or removed, only a small fraction (1/N) of keys need to be remapped, making it highly efficient for scaling out.
interactive_questions.theory_explanation: Consistent hashing maps data and servers to a circular ring. A key is assigned to the first server encountered moving clockwise. This minimizes disruption during scaling.
interactive_questions.real_world_analogy: Think of seating people at round tables. If a new table is added, you don't reshuffle everyone in the room; you only move a few people nearby to the new table.

interactive_questions.title: API Gateway Architecture
interactive_questions.prompt: Configure an API Gateway to route requests to microservices, handle authentication, and aggregate responses.
interactive_questions.question: Which of the following is NOT typically a responsibility of an API Gateway?
interactive_questions.explanation: An API Gateway acts as a reverse proxy to route requests and handle cross-cutting concerns (auth, rate limiting), but it should not serve as the primary persistent data store.
interactive_questions.theory_explanation: An API Gateway sits between clients and backend services. It acts as a single entry point, providing routing, composition, and protocol translation, simplifying client interactions with microservices.
interactive_questions.real_world_analogy: An API Gateway is like a hotel concierge. Instead of you finding the kitchen for food, the laundry for clothes, and the bellhop for luggage individually, you ask the concierge who handles routing your requests to the right departments.

critical_concepts.elaboration: System Design is the process of defining the architecture, modules, interfaces, and data for a system to satisfy specified requirements. In distributed systems, it focuses on scalability, reliability, and performance.

Designing distributed systems involves balancing trade-offs, such as consistency vs. availability (CAP theorem), latency vs. throughput, and data partitioning strategies (sharding, replication) to handle massive scale.

interactive_questions.title: System Design: Overview
interactive_questions.prompt: Explore the fundamental concepts of designing large-scale, highly available distributed systems.
interactive_questions.question: According to the CAP theorem, which two guarantees can a distributed system realistically provide simultaneously when a network partition occurs?
interactive_questions.explanation: Because network partitions (P) are inevitable in distributed systems, you must choose between providing Consistency (C) or Availability (A) during a partition. Thus, the system can either be CP or AP.
interactive_questions.theory_explanation: System Design is the process of architecting distributed systems. A key principle is the CAP Theorem: you can only have two of Consistency, Availability, and Partition Tolerance. In reality, Partitions (network failures) will happen, so systems must choose between prioritizing Consistency (everyone sees the same data, but some requests might fail) or Availability (all requests succeed, but some users might see stale data).
interactive_questions.real_world_analogy: Imagine a bank with two branches that lose phone connection (Partition). If a customer wants to withdraw money, the bank can either refuse (prioritizing Consistency so accounts don't overdraw) or allow it (prioritizing Availability but risking overdraws until the phones work again).

interactive_questions.title: Architectural Topology Challenge
interactive_questions.prompt: Review the architectural requirement: A highly decoupled system where components react to state changes asynchronously without direct point-to-point connections.
interactive_questions.question: Which of the following visual options correctly identifies the architectural paradigm?
interactive_questions.explanation: Event-Driven Architecture decouples publishers from subscribers using a central message broker, fulfilling the requirement.
interactive_questions.theory_explanation: In an event-driven system, the state is communicated via events that components produce and consume asynchronously, removing tight coupling.
interactive_questions.real_world_analogy: Event-driven architecture is like a busy restaurant kitchen (the broker). Waiters drop order tickets (events) on the rail, and independent chefs (consumers) react without the waiter explicitly managing them.
